title: Guidelines
hookLine: seventh point: do everything with one intention; begin and end the day with it

lines: THE FIRST THOUGHT OF THE DAY.
THE SEVENTH POINT TAKES THEM BACK.
cards: Before your feet hit the floor this morning, what was the first thing in your head? A deadline. A phone.
Last night's argument. And the last thing at night is often whatever happened to be on the screen. Both ends of the day get handed to whatever shows up first.
The seventh and last point of mind training, lojong, takes those two moments back on purpose.
Its guidelines are short, and one is almost too simple to notice: do everything with one intention, and begin and end the day with it.

teach.b: First, what the guidelines are: short lines for ordinary life, after the cushion. Not special practice; the dishes, the inbox, the commute.
Second, one intention. A line usually given as: do all activities with one intention.
Teachers explain the intention as bodhicitta, the wish to wake up for the sake of others, the same wish all of mind training has been growing.
One thread runs through everything, so typing an email and sitting in meditation become the same work, done for the same reason. Third, two activities, one at the beginning and one at the end.
In the morning, set the intention before the day sets it for you. At night, look back.
Teachers describe the evening as a gentle review: be glad for what went well, be honest about what didn't, and set the intention again for tomorrow.

teach.h: ONE AT THE START, ONE AT THE END.
teach.b: No punishment in it, just a clear look and a fresh start. Fourth, steadiness.
Another line of point seven is usually given as: whichever of the two occurs, be patient. Commentaries read the two as good fortune and bad.
Neither a good day nor a hard one is a reason to drop the thread. The point isn't a perfect day; it's that the thread holds either way.
And with that, the seven points credited to Chekawa are complete: the basics, the main practice, trouble as the path, a whole life's practice, checking yourself, commitments, and now guidelines.
Tomorrow the block turns from training the mind to bringing the body down to the floor.

how: Practitioners of Tibetan mind training often set the wish to benefit others on waking and review the day before sleep, rejoicing in what went well and regretting what did not, then renewing the intention.

o: the seventh point: short lines for living mind training daily
a teacher's rulebook for how monks spend every hour
advice on which meditation posture suits which person

games.q: the seventh point: tap the pairs.
p: look back, then set it again
be patient, good day or bad

s: the seventh point is only about formal meditation
its guidelines are for ordinary life: the dishes, the inbox, the commute.
the guidelines say to begin and end the day with the intention
one activity at the beginning, one at the end.
the evening review is meant to punish the day's mistakes
it's a clear look: glad for what went well, honest about what didn't, then a fresh start.

games.q: it's night. you set one intention this morning and kept it about half the day. the seventh point says to end the day with it. what do you do?
o: skip the review; it would only feel bad.
look back honestly, glad and sorry, then set it again.
games.why: teachers describe the evening that way: rejoice in what went well, regret what didn't, renew the intention. no perfect days required.

practice: Run back over the day so far, the way the evening review does: find one moment you're glad of and stay with it a breath, then one that didn't go well, and see it plainly, without scolding.
Then put one intention into a few plain words for what's left of the day, something like: to be of use to someone. Hold it gently while you breathe.

wordCard.voice: Guidelines. The seventh point of mind training: everything done with one intention, set in the morning and renewed at night. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit bodhicitta: the mind set on awakening for the sake of others, the intention mind training keeps returning to.

carryVoice: Your line: one intention. Set in the morning, looked back on at night. See you tomorrow.
